lines.text: Build a real, bounded queue for one connection's own outgoing messages, with a real cap on how many it holds.
Fill it to exactly that cap, then push one more. What happens to that extra message?
It's turned away outright.
The queue's own length never grows past the cap it was given.

lines.text: A real peer connects, then deliberately sends nothing at all, the way a slow, stalling attacker would.
The other side sets a real deadline on how long it will wait. Does it wait forever anyway, or does that deadline actually fire?
It actually fires.
Right on schedule, closing the connection to a peer that never sent a single byte.

lines.text: Run it for real: the real deadline fired right on schedule,
closing a connection whose peer had sent nothing at all — confirmed directly, by measuring the real elapsed time.
This protocol's own standard makes a specific claim about how long one side may leave its own receiving window shut.
What does it actually say?
Indefinitely.
As long as it keeps answering the other side's own probes, the standard itself allows the wait.
The standard's own words: one side may leave its receiving window closed indefinitely,
as long as it keeps answering the sender's own probes — not reading is a real, sanctioned way to say not yet.
Stop reading to say not yet, cap a queue to say no more than this, set a real deadline to say not forever:
that's overload handled as an explicit, deliberate choice, never something that simply happens on its own.

lines.text: So, pulling this topic together: not reading a real connection genuinely closes its own window and blocks the other side, exactly as the standard itself says is allowed, indefinitely.
A real bounded queue enforces its own cap by genuinely turning away the next push once it's full.
And a real deadline genuinely fires against a peer that may never send anything at all, closing the connection rather than waiting on it forever.
